rv.q: MRS. DOUBTFIRE brings big laughs, dazzling quick changes, and plenty of heart to Bass Concert Hall, reminding us that families may change shape while love remains.
Smith is a whirlwind of energy from the moment the show begins until curtain call.
Ultimately, Mrs. Doubtfire is exactly what it sets out to be: a high-energy, sentimental night of theater.
Mrs. Doubtfire may not push any theatrical boundaries, but it does succeed in delivering a fun night out.
Doubtfire works because of Craig Allen Smith'
Its desperation for laughs (which don't come easily) makes it seem jolting when they suddenly stomp on the brakes for an emotional scene.
Director Steve Edlund keeps the pace snappy and the energy vibrant throughout the show’s two-hour-and-40-minute running time.
Propelled by funny moments and highly entertaining musical numbers, "MRS. DOUBTFIRE" conveys the story of a parent attempting to obtain a deeper understanding of his family…and of himself.
Mrs. Doubtfire is humorous, madcap fun for the entire family, and it’s a stellar addition to the Arts Center’s Broadway showcase.
Many of the songs are quite touching, particularly Miranda's heartrending and nostalgic ballad 'Let Go,' and there are plenty of laughs.
The musical captures most of the plot of the film through the first act but the longish second half seems padded with too many songs that seem to repeat the same narratives.

Measured as a work of musical theater, however, “Mrs. Doubtfire” falls short in a number of ways, from its forgettable score to its flimsy sets to the cringe-inducing quantity of corn in a sizable chunk of Act One.
The songs (music and lyrics by Wayne Kirkpatrick and Karey Kirkpatrick) are acceptable but instantly forgettable.

cn.t: This crowd-pleasing adaptation delivers nostalgic fun and laughs anchored by an energetic lead performance, though critics find the score forgettable and the show rarely transcends its source material.
